title: Lay aside all earthly cares
hookLine: in the Cherubic hymn of the Liturgy, the people join the angels

lines: THE BREAD AND WINE CARRIED THROUGH.
cards: Partway through the Orthodox Divine Liturgy, the singing slows right down. The choir begins a hymn so drawn out that a single word can take a long breath to sing. A door in the screen of icons opens.
The clergy come out carrying the bread and wine for communion, walk them through the church with candles and incense, then back through the central doors to the altar.
And the words the choir is singing ask everyone standing there to do something hard. Put it all down. Not later.
Now. Today's word is the hymn's own phrase: lay aside all earthly cares.

teach.b: In substance it says: we who, in a mystery, represent the cherubim, and sing the thrice-holy hymn to the life-giving Trinity, let us now lay aside all earthly cares, so that we may receive the King of all, escorted unseen by the hosts of angels.
Alleluia. Look at what that claims. The people in the room, tired, distracted, holding coats and children, stand for the cherubim, angels the Bible places close to God.
The thrice-holy hymn is the song Isaiah heard the seraphim crying to one another in his vision: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory."
The Greek word for care in the hymn is merimna: worry, the pull of a divided mind. The Bible knows that pull. In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says, "Take therefore no thought for the morrow."
And Peter's first letter says, "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you." None of these says your cares don't matter. Peter says where to throw them.

teach.h: A BAG SET DOWN AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: The hymn says to lay them aside for now, like a bag set down at a door, so you can be fully in the room. They'll still be there when the service ends. But for a few minutes, they won't be running it.

how: In the Orthodox Divine Liturgy the choir sings the Cherubic Hymn while the clergy carry the bread and wine in procession, the Great Entrance; the people stand, and some cross themselves and bow as the gifts pass.

games.q: what does “lay aside all earthly cares” mean?
o: set your worries down for now, to be fully present
stop caring what happens in the world
give away everything you own to follow God

games.q: the Cherubic Hymn — tap the pairs.
p: in a mystery, represent the cherubim
casting all your care upon him

s: the Cherubic Hymn says your worries don't matter
it asks the people to lay them aside for now, to receive the King of all.
the thrice-holy song comes from Isaiah's vision
holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
in the hymn, only the clergy stand for the angels
the whole gathering sings: we who, in a mystery, represent the cherubim.

games.q: the choir starts the Cherubic Hymn. your mind is on tomorrow's bills. what does the hymn ask of you?
o: work the bills out first, then sing.
lay that care aside for now, and join the song.
games.why: let us now lay aside all earthly cares. not forever, and not by pretending: set down, so the hands are free to receive.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, name the care that's heaviest right now, just one, and feel its weight for a breath, as if it were in your hands.
Then slowly set it down beside you, like a bag on the floor by a door; it isn't gone, and you can pick it up after.
If you pray, hand it over with Peter's line, casting all your care upon him; if you don't, simply sit with empty hands.

wordCard.voice: Lay aside all earthly cares. The line from the Cherubic Hymn that asks the people to set their worries down and sing with the angels.

orig.note: Greek for care or worry: the word the hymn asks the people to lay aside.

carryVoice: Your line: lay aside all cares. Set down is not the same as thrown away. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, the Cherubic Hymn
